Hook: Cheltenham, in England, on the morning of the thirteenth of August, 1856. The British Association for the Advancement of Science is meeting in the town. At breakfast in a hotel, a Welsh ironmaster sits down opposite a friend and says, as the inventor himself later told it: do you know, there is actually a fellow come down from London to read a paper on the manufacture of malleable iron without fuel? Ha, ha, ha! The man sitting next to his friend was the fellow: Henry Bessemer. And that morning he read the paper.

Iron from a blast furnace, pig iron, carries about five per cent carbon. That makes it hard and brittle: you can cast it, but you cannot roll it into rails or plates. To make it tough, the carbon had to come out, and that took hours of stirring in a furnace, by hand, a few hundredweight at a time. Bessemer's idea was to blow cold air through the molten iron. The oxygen burns the carbon, and the burning gives off so much heat that the iron gets hotter, not colder. No fuel, no furnace: the impurity is the fuel. What is left is steel. His first vessel converted about 7 hundredweight of pig iron, some 356 kilograms, in 30 minutes. Within a generation, steel went from a craftsman's metal to the stuff of rails, ships and bridges.

Today the world makes steel by the billion tonnes. In 2025, about 1,849 million tonnes of it. Even more cement: some 3.8 billion tonnes, about twice the weight of the steel. And 74 million tonnes of new aluminium. Spread over everyone, about 209 kilograms of finished steel a year for every person on Earth: in buildings, cars, pipes, cans and machines.

And they are astonishingly cheap. Here is what a kilogram costs, on a scale where each step is ten times the last. Crushed stone, the gravel in every road and every slab of concrete: about 2 cents a kilogram at the quarry. Cement: about 16 cents. Steel sheet, rolled and coiled: about 94 cents. For comparison, a kilogram of bananas in an American shop: 1 dollar 44. Steel, cheaper than fruit. Aluminium, the dear one of the family, about 3 dollars 28.

These are the materials everything else is made of, made in plants that cost billions and last half a century, and yet the companies that make them mostly earn thin and unreliable profits. Industry, Built. Part eleven: heavy materials. Why do the things everything is made of earn so little?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: a mill in a glut.

Play it yourself. You run an integrated steel mill: a blast furnace that turns iron ore into molten iron, and a steel shop beside it. It can make about 3 million tonnes of steel a year. Each tonne costs about 520 dollars in ore, coke, power and everything else that goes into it. And 750 million dollars a year must be paid whether you make anything or not: wages, maintenance, the pensions of past workers, the interest on what the plant cost. So at full output you break even at about 770 dollars a tonne. One more fact about a blast furnace: it is not a tap. Below about three quarters of its capacity it does not run well, and to stop it you bank it, keep it warm and idle, which still costs about half the fixed costs, and bringing it back costs millions.

Now a glut arrives. Over the next two years, quarter by quarter, the market price falls from 880 dollars a tonne to 620, below your break-even, before it recovers. And your customers' orders shrink, to 60 per cent of what you can make. You have three choices. A: run full anyway, sell what is ordered and push the rest out at fifteen per cent below the market. B: cut your output to what is ordered, though never below the furnace's three quarters. C: bank the furnace in the quarters when orders fall below three quarters, and restart it when they come back. Pause, and choose.

Here is how each choice plays out, quarter by quarter, in millions of dollars. In the good quarters, all three make money. Then the glut. Running full loses money, but every tonne still sells for more than its ore and coke, so each extra tonne cuts the loss a little. Cutting output saves on ore and coke, but the fixed costs do not shrink. Banking the furnace stops the bleeding from steel, but half the fixed costs go on, and the restart costs more. The totals: running full, about 308 million dollars lost; cutting output, 357 million; banking, 317 million. For one mill, on its own, the least bad choice is to keep the furnace running and sell at whatever price it takes.

But you are not the only mill. Every mill in the glut does the same sum, and reaches the same answer. If all of them run full and push their extra tonnes onto the market, the price falls much further: in this model, to about 482 dollars a tonne. Now running full loses about 650 million dollars, twice as much, and banking the furnace becomes the least bad choice. And the longer the glut lasts, the better banking looks. What is best for each mill alone makes the glut deeper for all of them. That is why gluts in heavy industry last: furnaces keep running at a loss, each hoping the others will stop first.

And what did real mills do? In 2025, a hard year for American integrated steel, Cleveland-Cliffs decided to idle or close 6 of its operations: it banked the blast furnace at Dearborn in Michigan, closed three older plants for good, and restarted a furnace in Ohio. US Steel, bought that June by Nippon Steel, halted a mill in Illinois but kept it ready to restart. Cliffs lost about 1.5 billion dollars that year. Nucor, whose mills melt scrap in electric furnaces, earned 1.7 billion. Why such different fortunes? It starts with the two ways of making steel.
Routes: There are two ways to make steel. The first is Bessemer's descendant: the integrated mill. According to Cleveland-Cliffs, America's largest integrated steelmaker, a tonne of its steel takes about 1.4 tonnes of iron ore pellets, a third of a tonne of coke, which is coal baked in ovens, about 0.5 tonnes of coal in all, and a little scrap. In the blast furnace, the burning coke strips the oxygen from the iron ore, and molten iron runs out at the bottom, carrying four or five per cent carbon. A ladle carries it to the converter, where pure oxygen is blown in, as Bessemer blew air, and the carbon burns away in minutes. Out comes steel, cast into slabs. The carbon that took the oxygen from the ore leaves as carbon dioxide: about 2.3 tonnes for every tonne of steel, by the steel industry's own count.

The second way skips the ore altogether. A minimill melts scrap: old cars, demolished buildings, the offcuts of factories. Nucor says it takes about 1.1 tonnes of scrap, or substitutes for it, to make a tonne of steel. The furnace is a bowl with three graphite electrodes in its lid. Lower them, switch on, and an electric arc hotter than the surface of the sun melts the charge in under an hour. Pour, cast, and you have steel. Because nobody has to pull oxygen out of ore, the carbon dioxide is far lower: about 0.7 tonnes a tonne, most of it from the power station. Some electric furnaces are fed with iron made from ore using natural gas instead of coke, which sits in between.

Which way a country makes its steel depends on what it has. China makes almost nine tenths of its steel from ore, in blast furnaces. So do Japan and South Korea. Worldwide, about 30 per cent comes from electric furnaces. But in the United States it is 71 per cent, and in Türkiye more still. The difference is scrap. An old industrial country is a mine of old steel: cars reach the end of their lives, buildings come down, and American scrapyards recycle almost all of it. In the United States, just 2 companies still run blast furnaces; 47 companies run 102 minimills. A country that has only just built its cities, like China, has not yet had time to throw much steel away.
Tonne: Chapter three. A ton of steel and its dollar.

Take a ton of steel from Nucor, America's largest steelmaker, which makes all of it in electric furnaces. In 2025, its mills sold steel for 1,008 dollars a ton on average. Each ton took about 1.1 tons of scrap, which cost 392 dollars a ton: about 385 dollars of metal in every ton sold. The rest, about 623 dollars, is what the industry calls the metal spread. It has to pay for the electricity, the electrodes and alloys, the wages, the upkeep, the wear on the plant, and then, if anything is left, the profit. A steelmaker is a business that buys metal, adds heat and know-how, and lives on the spread.

The spread moves a great deal. Here is Nucor's steel price, year by year since 2018, and the scrap in each ton. In 2020, with the pandemic, the spread was about 386 dollars. In 2021 and 2022, as the economy reopened and steel ran short, prices rose far faster than scrap, and the spread more than doubled, to over 841 dollars. Nucor's profit went from 0.7 billion dollars in 2020 to 7.6 billion in 2022, ten times as much, and back down to 1.7 billion in 2025. A few hundred dollars of spread, on twenty-odd million tons, decides everything.

Now the same year for an integrated mill. Nucor sold its mills' steel at about 1,008 dollars a ton and earned 1.7 billion dollars. Cleveland-Cliffs, with its blast furnaces, sold its steel for 1,005 dollars a ton on average, almost exactly the same price, and lost money on it before it paid a cent of interest: its gross margin was minus 5 per cent. And 2025 was not a bad year for prices: the benchmark, hot-rolled coil, averaged 851 dollars, up from 772, lifted, Cliffs says, by tariffs on imports. Same product, same price, opposite results. The difference is in the costs, and above all in the costs that do not go away.

Step back and look at the price of steel since 1947, after taking out inflation. It spikes in booms: 1974, 2008, 2021. But over the long run it goes nowhere: in 2025 a ton cost, in real terms, about what it did in 1960, when the index stood at 1.0 times today's. Steelmakers have become far more productive, and almost none of it has turned into a higher price. Competition has handed it to the people who buy steel.
MustRun: Chapter four. A plant that must run.

Here is the problem in one picture. On the left, how much of the mill is being used; up the side, what a tonne costs to make. For the integrated mill of chapter one, nearly a third of the cost of a tonne, at full output, is fixed: it is there whether the furnace runs or not. For a minimill, about a sixth. Now let orders fall. At eighty per cent, the integrated mill's tonne costs noticeably more. At sixty per cent, the fixed costs are spread over so few tonnes that each one costs hundreds of dollars more than at full output. The minimill's costs rise too, but far more gently. That is why a heavy plant wants to run full at almost any price, and why an industry full of them keeps producing into a glut.

How full are American mills, in practice? Here is the Federal Reserve's measure for the whole industry since 1972. In good years, eighty or ninety per cent. In the slump of 1982, 50 per cent; in 2009, after the financial crisis, 51. Nucor's mills follow the same tide: ninety-seven per cent in 2004, 54 per cent in 2009, 83 per cent in 2025. The tide is the economy: steel goes into buildings, cars and machines, which are exactly what people stop buying in a recession.

And so the profits of steelmakers swing like few others. Here are four American steelmakers over ten years. A few hundred million dollars a year in the quiet years. Then 2021 and 2022: Nucor earns 7.6 billion dollars in a single year, US Steel 4.2 billion. And then back down, and for the blast-furnace companies, below zero: Cleveland-Cliffs lost money in 2024 and again in 2025. A business with big fixed costs magnifies every swing in price: a little more price falls straight to profit, and a little less comes straight out of it.
Minimills: The minimill is the most famous story in business schools of an industry overturned from below. The Harvard professor Clayton Christensen made it his textbook case. Steel products form a ladder, from the cheapest, rebar, the ribbed bars buried in concrete, up through bars and angles, structural beams, and at the top, the flat sheet that goes into cars and refrigerators, where the margins were best. In the 1960s the big integrated mills made all of it. The first minimills could only make the bottom rung. Their scrap steel was not good enough for anything else. Nucor's first, at Darlington in South Carolina, started in 1969 to supply the company's own joist plants. The integrated mills were glad to give rebar up: its margins were thin. Then the minimills got better, and climbed: bars and angles in the seventies and eighties, beams, when Nucor and Japan's Yamato Kogyo built a beam mill in Arkansas in 1988, and finally sheet, when at the end of the 1980s Nucor's mill at Crawfordsville, Indiana, became the first minimill in the world to make quality flat-rolled steel by casting thin slabs. At every step, the integrated mills retreated upward, to the business that was left, until there was little left to retreat to.

Here is the result in one series: the share of American steel made in electric furnaces. 38 per cent in 1992. 47 per cent in 2000. 68 per cent in 2019. And 71 per cent in 2025. The blast furnace, which made almost all of America's steel for a century, now makes less than a third of it.

And here it is in two companies. In 2010, Nucor and US Steel, a corporation established in 1901, the giant of American steel for most of the century since, had about the same revenue. By 2024, Nucor's was twice US Steel's. Add up the profits from 2010 to 2024: Nucor, about 30 billion dollars. US Steel, about 3 billion. In June 2025, US Steel was bought by Japan's Nippon Steel, with the American government's approval and conditions.
Glut: Chapter six. Half the world's steel.

Now the world. World steel production grew fast after the war, stalled for twenty years from the mid-1970s at around seven or eight hundred million tonnes, and then took off again. Almost all of the take-off was one country. In 1995 China made about 13 per cent of the world's steel. By 2025 it made 52 per cent: 961 million tonnes, more than the rest of the world put together. The cities, railways, factories and apartment towers of the fastest build-out in history were made of it.

Here are the ten biggest producers in 2025. China, then a long way behind, India, with 165 million tonnes and growing fastest, then the United States and Japan, each around eighty. Per person, China now uses more than twice as much steel as the United States, 562 kilograms a year against 262, and India about a fifth as much as China. India is where the next great build-out is happening.

Then the build-out ended. From 2021, China's property market turned down, and with it the demand for steel. The steel China used fell from 954 million tonnes in 2021 to 796 million in 2025, a drop larger than everything the United States uses in a year. China's production fell much less. Mills kept running, for all the reasons of the last two chapters. So the steel went abroad. China's exports went from about 66 million tonnes in 2021 to 134 million in 2025, roughly doubling. That is more steel than the whole United States makes in a year, offered on the world market, mostly at prices other mills could not match.

So the glut became a trade war. China's surplus flowed to every market with a port. And the walls went up. The United States had put a twenty-five per cent tariff on most imported steel in 2018. In March 2025 it removed every exception, and in June it doubled the tariff, to 50 per cent. The European Union, which bought about 44 million tonnes of steel from outside in 2025, kept quotas and began charging a carbon price at its border in 2026. Steel is one of the few industries every government wants to have at home: for defence, for jobs, and for the towns built around the mills. That is one more reason capacity does not close.
Cement: Chapter seven. Cement: a circle on the map.

Cement is made in a simpler way than steel, but at a temperature just as fierce. Limestone and clay come from a quarry, usually right beside the plant, and are crushed into a powder. The powder falls down a tower, warmed by the hot gases coming up, and into the kiln: a steel tube lined with brick, as long as a football field, turning slowly and sloping down towards a flame at about fourteen hundred and fifty degrees. What comes out are grey nodules called clinker, which are ground with a little gypsum into cement. Mix cement with sand, gravel and water, and you have concrete. The chemistry has a catch. Heating limestone splits it into lime and carbon dioxide. About half a tonne of carbon dioxide comes out of the rock itself for every tonne of clinker, before a single tonne of fuel is burned.

The world made about 3.8 billion tonnes of cement in 2025. China, 1.7 billion, nearly half; India, 470 million; Viet Nam, a hundred million; the United States, 84 million. Unlike steel, almost every country makes its own. America has 97 cement plants in thirty-four states. A tonne sold for about 160 dollars at the plant in 2025, up from 127 in 2021, and most of it went to companies that mix concrete and deliver it in those turning drums. Some comes in by ship, to coastal terminals. Almost none travels far by road. And that is the whole economics of cement.

Here is why. A tonne of cement is heavy and cheap, so trucking it eats the price quickly. In the European Commission's files, trucking cement in 1989 cost about seven hundredths of an ECU, Europe's accounting unit, per tonne and kilometre, when a tonne sold for about 70 ECU: five hundred kilometres of road added half the price. So picture two plants, three hundred kilometres apart. A tonne leaves each gate at the same cost, and costs more the further it is trucked. Each plant is the cheapest supplier in its own circle, out to the border halfway between them. And within its circle, a plant only has to beat its rival's delivered cost, which is highest right at its own gate. So the margin is fattest close to home, and vanishes at the border. Every cement plant is a small monopoly on a circle of map. Nationally, the four largest American cement firms sell about half the cement, and the four largest concrete firms just fifteen per cent of the concrete. But nobody buys concrete nationally. Locally, a builder may have two or three suppliers to choose from.
Cartel: Chapter eight. The home market rule.

Circles that overlap are a temptation. Where two plants' markets meet, they compete on price, and a producer with a spare kiln can always ship to a neighbour's town by sea or by rail. In Western Europe, the cement industry's leaders found a way round that. The European Commission later established that at a meeting on the fourteenth of January 1983 they agreed a rule of, in its words, non-transhipment to home markets: no exports into another country's market that might destabilise it. Each country's producers kept their own circle. In the Commission's file there is a handwritten note of one meeting. It reads: Home market principle OK. But is it easily complied with, in Belgium?

On the thirtieth of November 1994, the Commission fined 42 cement companies and trade associations a total of about 250 million euros. The names on the decision include Holderbank, Lafarge, Heidelberger Zement, Italcementi, Buzzi and Vicat: many of them still names, or the roots of names, among the biggest cement companies today. In 2000, a European court cut the fines by almost 140 million euros, mostly because of flaws in how the case was run, not because the agreement had not existed. Cement is prone to it, for the reasons this chapter and the last describe: a few plants in each region, a product that is the same whoever makes it, heavy fixed costs, and prices that everyone can see.

Today the circles are bought, sold and swapped like pieces on a board. In June 2025, Holcim, the Swiss cement group, spun off its North American business as a separate company, Amrize, with 18 cement plants. Martin Marietta sold its South Texas cement plant to CRH for 2.1 billion dollars in 2024, and agreed to swap its other Texas cement plant with QUIKRETE for quarries. A company that owned both chose to keep the stone and sell the cement. We will see why in chapter eleven.
Intermission: An intermission: seventy-five years of the world's steel. The post-war boom, when Europe and Japan rebuilt and America made cars by the million. The oil shocks of the 1970s, and then twenty years in which the world made about the same amount of steel every year, and the old steel towns of America and Europe shut their furnaces one after another. The collapse of the Soviet Union, and of the mills that had served it. Then China, whose output went from about 127 million tonnes in 2000 to more than a billion in 2020. And the peak, so far, in 2021. Look at the shape: long flat stretches, and one great climb that was almost entirely one country.

The story so far. The materials the world is built from are among the cheapest things it buys by weight. Steel is made two ways, from ore and coal, or from scrap and electricity. A steelmaker lives on the spread between its price and its metal. Its fixed costs make it run in good times and bad, so gluts last and profits swing. The minimills climbed from the bottom of the market to the top. China makes half the world's steel. And cement, which travels badly, gives every plant its own small territory. Next: the metal that is really electricity, the box, the quarry, and the carbon.
Aluminium: Chapter nine. Electricity in solid form.

Aluminium is the third heavy material, and a strange one. It starts as bauxite, a red ore, which is refined into a white powder, alumina, aluminium bound to oxygen. To pull the oxygen off, alumina is dissolved in molten salt in long rows of pots, and an enormous electric current is passed through it. Liquid aluminium collects at the bottom. It takes about 13,880 kilowatt-hours of electricity to make one tonne, on the industry's world average for 2025, down from almost seventeen thousand in 1980. So a smelter making half a million tonnes a year draws about 792 megawatts, day and night: the output of a large power station, all for one factory. Alcoa says electricity is about 24 per cent of what its smelters spend. Aluminium is, in effect, electricity in solid form.

Because power is most of the cost you can control, smelters go wherever electricity is cheap and plentiful: to the rivers of Canada, Norway and Iceland, to the gas fields of the Gulf, and above all, this century, to China. In 2000 China made about 11 per cent of the world's new aluminium. By 2025, 60 per cent. America went the other way. Its smelters made about 4.7 million tonnes in 1980. In 2025, 0.66 million, from 6 smelters, two of them shut. As American power got dearer relative to other places, the pots went cold.

Electricity in solid form also means that a shock to energy is a shock to aluminium. The Gulf states, with their cheap gas, made about one tonne in every twelve of the world's aluminium. Here is their output, month by month. In April 2026, with the region at war and the Strait of Hormuz shut, as in Part eight, it fell from about 513 thousand tonnes a month to 274. And the world price, which had been creeping up, jumped, to 3,658 dollars a tonne in May 2026. Americans paid more still: behind a fifty per cent tariff, aluminium in the United States averaged 180 cents a pound in 2025, against about 119 cents in London.
Packaging: Chapter ten. Boxes, cans and bottles.

The heavy-materials family has a lighter branch: packaging. The boxes, cans and bottles that everything else is shipped and sold in. In the United States, the four largest firms make about half of all corrugated boxes, two thirds of the containerboard they are made from, 62 per cent of metal cans, and 88 per cent of glass bottles and jars, which come from just 22 firms. Like steel, these are continuous processes: a paper machine, a glass furnace, a can line, running day and night, cheapest per box or per can when they are big and full. That pushes the industry into fewer, larger hands.

And the hands keep getting fewer. In July 2024, Ireland's Smurfit Kappa and America's WestRock closed their combination, making Smurfit Westrock, with about 31 billion dollars of sales in 2025, one of the largest box makers in the world. Six months later, in January 2025, International Paper bought Britain's DS Smith. Bigger, though, has not meant richer. Over the last five years Smurfit Westrock kept about 5 cents of every dollar of sales as profit, International Paper about 1, after losses on what it sold and closed. The best of the group, Packaging Corporation of America, North America's third-largest containerboard maker, about 10.

There is a reason for the mergers. Here is the output of America's pulp, paper and board mills since 1972. It peaked in 1995, and by 2025 it had fallen by 46 per cent. Newspapers, magazines, letters and office paper moved to screens, and many of the mills that made paper for them closed. Boxes held up better, and the producer price of a box more than doubled between 2000 and 2025. A shrinking industry with a sturdier corner consolidates: the survivors buy each other, close the weakest mills, and try to keep the rest full.
Quarry: Chapter eleven. The quarry with a permit.

The humblest heavy material is stone. America quarries about 1.5 billion tonnes of crushed stone a year, from 3,500 quarries, at about 18 dollars a tonne: the gravel under every road and inside every concrete slab. It is so heavy for its price that it barely travels. Vulcan Materials, the largest producer, says about eighty per cent of its stone goes straight from the quarry to the customer by truck, and that transport costs can quickly exceed the cost of the stone itself. Truck a load a few dozen miles and its price has risen by a quarter; a hundred miles or so, and it has doubled. Every quarry serves its own neighbourhood, and the nearest quarry to a growing city is worth a great deal.

Now watch what that does to the price. Here is a tonne of crushed stone, in today's dollars, since 1900. It peaked around 1934, and then for some sixty years got cheaper, as quarries mechanised, down to about 11 dollars in 2000. And then, unlike steel, it climbed, year after year, to about 19 dollars in 2025, the highest since 1953. The government's own geologists give a reason: shortages near cities, because of zoning and because the land is worth more as houses. New quarries end up further away, and trucking makes the old ones near town ever more valuable. Nobody can open a rival quarry next door. The permit is the moat.

Here is a ton of Vulcan's stone in 2025. It sold for about 22 dollars, after taking out the cost of delivery. Of that, 8.66 dollars was gross profit: about two fifths of the price, on a product that is, after all, broken rock. And Vulcan reports 16.6 billion tons of proven and probable reserves, at its 2025 pace about 73 years of selling, in quarries already permitted, near the cities that will need them. That is why Martin Marietta, which owned both, chose to keep the quarries and sell or swap away its cement plants. In heavy materials, the money is where something cannot be copied: here, a hole in the ground with a permit, close to town.
Carbon: Heavy materials have one more cost that does not show up in their price. The world emits about 39 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year from fossil fuels and industry. Cement's chemistry alone, the carbon dioxide driven out of limestone in the kiln, is about 1.5 billion of it, before counting the fuel. Steel, by the industry's own count, emitted about 4.1 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases in 2024, some 7 to 8 per cent of all the world's. These are two of the largest sources of emissions there are, and among the hardest to remove.

Why so hard? Because in a blast furnace the carbon is not just fuel. It is the chemistry. Iron ore is iron bound to oxygen, and carbon is what takes the oxygen away, leaving as carbon dioxide: about 1.2 tonnes for every tonne of iron, from the reaction alone. There is another molecule that can take the oxygen: hydrogen. Then what leaves is water. It takes about 54 kilograms of hydrogen per tonne of iron. Made from water with electricity, that is nearly 3 megawatt-hours, and at two to five dollars a kilogram, between 108 and 271 dollars a tonne, on a product that sells for about a thousand. Cement has no such swap: the carbon dioxide comes from the limestone itself. The answers are to use less clinker in each tonne, which American cement makers have done fast, 63 per cent of their shipments are now blended cements, and to capture what is left.

Who pays? Europe's answer is a price on carbon for its own plants, and, so that imports do not undercut them, a charge at the border. Under a 2023 regulation, importers of cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen have reported the carbon in their goods since October 2023, and from the first of January 2026 they must pay for it. And the bill for steel's own transition is enormous. The industry's association estimates about 1.2 trillion dollars for new and rebuilt plants, and two and a half to four trillion more for the energy and infrastructure around them. For an industry that, as this film has shown, earns thin and unreliable profits, that is the hardest question of all.
Landscape: Here is the landscape, as of November 2026. First the steelmakers, by the tonnes they made in 2025. The largest by far is China Baowu, with about 125 million tonnes, more than the whole of Japan. Then ArcelorMittal, based in Luxembourg, and Nippon Steel, which now includes US Steel. Seven of the top twelve are Chinese; India's Tata and JSW are climbing. The largest American, Nucor, comes in at about 22 million tonnes, sixteenth in the world.

Now the companies that file accounts in the United States, by revenue and by how much of each dollar they kept over five years. The steelmakers: Nucor and Steel Dynamics, the minimills, around 12 cents in the dollar over a boom and a bust; ArcelorMittal, the biggest; and Cleveland-Cliffs, with blast furnaces, near zero. Cement and stone: CRH, the largest of them all by revenue, Amrize, and Cemex; and the quarry owners, Vulcan and Martin Marietta, at 12 and 16 cents, the best of the large ones. Aluminium, Alcoa and Century, barely above zero. And packaging, from Packaging Corporation near the top to International Paper and O-I Glass near the bottom. Big, essential and, mostly, thin: the money sits with whoever has a moat, a permit near a city, a scrap-fed mill near its customers.

And what to watch. China's steel: its output was down almost three per cent in the first ten months of 2026, and how much of the rest it sends abroad. America's tariffs of fifty per cent on steel and aluminium, and what they do to prices at home. The Gulf's smelters, climbing back after the war. Building: data centres and factories, which Nucor says are driving its orders, against housing and roads. Carbon: Europe's border charge in its first year, and whether hydrogen steel gets built. And China's demand for steel, which brings us to our call.
Called: Part eleven's forecast to test comes from the steel industry itself. Every October, the World Steel Association publishes its forecast of steel demand for the year ahead, country by country. Here are its forecasts for China. In October 2022, it expected China's demand in 2023 to be flat. It fell more than two per cent. In October 2023, flat again for 2024. It fell more than five per cent. In October 2024, a fall of one per cent in 2025. The association's own later report gives the official figure: a fall of seven per cent. Called it? No, three years running. Each time, the people who know the industry best expected China's property slump to bottom out within a year. Each time it went on.

Now our own forecast, written down so you can check it. In October 2026, worldsteel forecast that China's steel demand would fall 2 per cent in 2026. We think it will turn out to have fallen by more than that. Its forecasts have erred on the high side three years running, and China's crude steel output in the first ten months of 2026 was 2.8 per cent below the year before. Against us: exports and factories have held up, and the figures get revised. We give it 70 per cent. We will check it against worldsteel's own report in April 2027, and report the answer, right or wrong.
